summary: Defines EAP-FAST, an Extensible Authentication Protocol method that sets up a TLS-protected tunnel between a peer and a server and authenticates both sides. Inside the tunnel it carries authentication data in type-length-value objects. This memo is informational, describing a vendor-originated method rather than an IETF standard.

plainLanguage.summary: Before two sides share secrets, they first build a locked tube between them. EAP-FAST makes that tube, then passes the proof of who you are safely through it.

questions: what is a pac in eap-fast
subtitle: An EAP method that builds a TLS tunnel first, then does password-style login safely inside it.

tldr.problem: Network access needs strong mutual authentication that still works with weak credentials such as passwords, resists eavesdropping and man-in-the-middle attacks, and is light enough for wireless devices.
tldr.mechanism: EAP-FAST first sets up a mutually authenticated TLS tunnel, optionally resumed quickly with a Protected Access Credential (PAC), then runs inner authentication and TLV messages inside that tunnel, bound to it with a Crypto-Binding TLV.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational RFC, not a standard, and it has been updated by RFC 8996 and RFC 9427.

today: RFC 4851 is an Informational RFC with no obsoleting RFC, and it is updated by RFC 8996 and RFC 9427. It does not specify an Internet standard of any kind.

sections.title: Goals of EAP-FAST
sections.content:
EAP-FAST (Flexible Authentication via Secure Tunneling) is an Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP) method. It establishes a Transport Layer Security (TLS) tunnel, using TLS 1.0, TLS 1.1 or a successor, and then exchanges Type-Length-Value (TLV) objects inside the tunnel to authenticate further.

The stated design goals are mutual authentication, immunity to passive dictionary attacks, immunity to man-in-the-middle attacks, flexibility to support most password interfaces (the RFC names MS-CHAP, LDAP and one-time passwords), and efficiency for wireless peers with limited computing and power. Secondary goals are flexibility to extend what happens inside the tunnel and minimal per-user state on the authentication server.

The state-saving trick is the Protected Access Credential (PAC): a shared secret plus an opaque element that the peer presents later, based on the TLS session ticket extension of RFC 4507.
sections.plainLanguage: The aim is a login that is safe even if your password is simple. The guard also hands you a special pass, so next time you can get in faster without the guard remembering you.

sections.title: Architecture and Layering
sections.content:
Four logical entities take part: the peer, the authenticator, the EAP-FAST server and the inner method server. They may be separate or combined. In typical 802.11 deployments the authenticator sits in an access point, while a RADIUS server may provide the EAP-FAST and inner method server roles.

The protocols are layered. EAP-FAST packets travel inside EAP, which needs a carrier such as EAP over LAN, RADIUS or Diameter. EAP-FAST packets carry TLS, TLS carries a TLV layer, and the TLV layer carries an inner EAP method or other TLV information. All conversation inside the protected tunnel must be encapsulated in TLVs.
sections.plainLanguage: It is like envelopes inside envelopes. The outer one gets the letter to the right office, the next one is locked, and the secret note sits in the innermost envelope.

sections.title: Phase 1 Tunnel and Phase 2 Authentication
sections.content:
The conversation has two phases. In Phase 1 the TLS handshake gives an authenticated key exchange and a protected tunnel. The server starts with an EAP-FAST Start packet that includes the version and an authority identity (A-ID), which hints which credential the peer should use. This specification is EAP-FAST version 1, and implementations MUST use a version field set to 1. Implementations MUST support three TLS ciphersuites, including TLS_RSA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA.

A peer holding a valid PAC puts the PAC-Opaque in the TLS SessionTicket extension of its ClientHello and finishes an abbreviated handshake. The PAC-Key is a 32-octet key from which the TLS master secret is derived. If resumption fails, the server can fall back to a full handshake.

In Phase 2 the peer and server exchange TLVs, optionally running one or more inner EAP methods in sequence, one after another and never in parallel. Phase 2 MUST NOT happen if the Phase 1 handshake fails, and it MUST end with a protected Result TLV exchange. After that the tunnel is closed and a clear text EAP-Success or EAP-Failure is sent.

EAP messages can be larger than the medium allows, so EAP-FAST has its own fragmentation using L, M and S flag bits and a four-octet TLS Message Length field. Each fragment is acknowledged by an empty response.
sections.plainLanguage: Step one: build the locked tunnel. Step two: inside it, prove who you are. At the end the tunnel closes and the guard tells everyone outside whether you got in.

sections.title: Packets and TLVs
sections.content:
An EAP-FAST packet has the EAP Code (1 Request, 2 Response), Identifier and Length fields, then Type 43, a Flags field (L M S R R), a 3-bit version and an optional four-octet Message Length that is present only when L is set. The Data field holds an encapsulated TLS record, or the A-ID in a Start message.

Inside the tunnel, each TLV begins with a Mandatory bit, a Reserved bit, a 14-bit TLV type and a 16-bit length. If a peer or server does not support a mandatory TLV, it MUST send a NAK TLV and ignore the others; an unsupported optional TLV can simply be ignored. The RFC says conforming implementations MUST support seven TLVs: Result, NAK, Error, EAP-Payload, Intermediate-Result, Crypto-Binding and Request-Action.

The Crypto-Binding TLV proves that both sides took part in both the tunnel setup and the inner authentications. It has a 32-octet nonce and a 20-octet Compound MAC, and it also confirms the negotiated version. The Error TLV uses codes 2001 (Tunnel_Compromise_Error) and 2002 (Unexpected_TLVs_Exchanged).
sections.plainLanguage: Every little message inside the tunnel has a label saying what it is and how long it is. If a label is marked must understand and you do not, you say so.

sections.title: Key Derivation and Crypto-Binding
sections.content:
The tunnel key block is made as in TLS, with an extra 40 octets called the session_key_seed. When a PAC is used, the TLS master secret is computed from the PAC-Key with a function called T-PRF, which is built on HMAC-SHA1 and produces 20 octets per block.

After each successful inner EAP method, an Intermediate Compound Key (IMCK) is derived from the previous seed and the inner method's Master Session Key, truncated or zero-padded to 32 octets. The Compound MAC in the Crypto-Binding TLV is HMAC-SHA1 over the TLV using the compound key. The final MSK and EMSK are 64 octets each, derived from the last S-IMCK. If no inner method succeeded, they come directly from the session_key_seed.
sections.plainLanguage: Each time you pass a check, the secret code for the tunnel is mixed again with a new ingredient. That way, nobody could swap in a different person halfway through.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The design focuses on wireless media, where anyone can capture traffic. Confidentiality and integrity come from TLS, and the Crypto-Binding TLV ties inner method endpoints to the tunnel endpoints. The protected Result TLV is the true success or failure indicator, and a peer SHOULD silently discard a clear text EAP Success or Failure that disagrees with it.

Method negotiation outside a tunnel is unprotected, so NAK packets can be spoofed to push toward weaker methods such as EAP-MD5. Separating the Phase 1 and Phase 2 servers is not recommended, since it can lose identity protection, allow offline dictionary attacks and weaken policy enforcement. The initial identity response is sent in cleartext, so no intermediary should trust it, and the RFC describes TLS renegotiation inside the tunnel to hide a client certificate. A PAC may be bound to a user identity, and a compliant implementation MUST validate it against Phase 2 identities. The RFC notes that denial-of-service by erroneous traffic remains possible.
sections.plainLanguage: The tunnel keeps eavesdroppers out, but the name you shout at the front door is still public. So the guard must not trust it until you prove it inside.
